[CONFLICT] The claim suggests that GDP per capita fails to capture subjective wellbeing, health, and social cohesion, but this is disputed because GDP per capita is widely recognized as an economic measure that intentionally excludes non-economic dimensions of wellbeing, making the claim a matter of interpretation rather than factual error.

C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: material living standards in market economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in market economies]

[PATH:empirical] Compare GDP per capita growth with direct measures of household consumption and real income growth (e.g., from national accounts and household surveys) across OECD countries post-1950. — If GDP per capita systematically underestimates improvements, we would expect direct consumption or income measures to show faster growth. Cross-checking these series can confirm or refute the bias.

[PATH:theoretical] Analyze the inclusion of non-market goods and quality improvements (e.g., health, education, environmental quality) in alternative welfare indices like the Human Development Index or the OECD Better Life Index. — GDP per capita omits many dimensions of material living standards. Testing whether these omitted factors have grown disproportionately in market economies would reveal whether the underestimation is systematic.

[PATH:literature] Review existing literature on the 'Beyond GDP' movement and studies that adjust GDP for changes in leisure, inequality, and household production (e.g., work by Stiglitz, Sen, Fitoussi). — A systematic underestimation would be supported if multiple adjusted measures consistently show larger improvements than GDP per capita. A literature review can synthesize evidence across countries and time periods.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita income inequality and non-market activities]

[PATH:literature] Piketty, T. (2014). Capital in the Twenty-First Century. Harvard University Press. — Provides extensive empirical data on income and wealth inequality across countries and time, directly challenging GDP per capita as a sufficient measure of economic well-being by showing how inequality distorts distributional outcomes.

[PATH:empirical] Stiglitz, J. E., Sen, A., & Fitoussi, J. P. (2009). Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress. — This influential report systematically critiques GDP per capita for ignoring non-market activities (e.g., household labor, volunteer work) and inequality, offering alternative metrics like the Better Life Index, which can be used to test the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] World Bank. (2023). World Development Indicators: Gini Index and GDP per capita. Washington, DC: World Bank. — Cross-country panel data on GDP per capita and Gini coefficients can be analyzed to test whether GDP per capita systematically fails to reflect well-being in high-inequality contexts, and to assess the magnitude of omitted non-market production through satellite accounts.

C007.subject: GDP per capita
C007.object: the variance in subjective wellbeing more than the variance in health or social cohesion
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita the variance in subjective wellbeing more than the variance in health or social cohesion]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index microdata and Gallup World Poll (OECD countries, 2000-2023) — Directly test the hypothesis by regressing subjective wellbeing (e.g., life satisfaction) against GDP per capita, health indicators (e.g., self-reported health), and social cohesion measures (e.g., trust, social support) to compare explained variance.

[PATH:empirical] Panel data from the World Values Survey and European Social Survey (2000-2020) — Allow for within-country and between-country variance decomposition to assess whether GDP per capita explains less variance in wellbeing than health or social cohesion over time within OECD nations.

[PATH:literature] Comparative meta-analysis of cross-national studies on determinants of subjective wellbeing (e.g., Easterlin paradox literature, Helliwell et al., World Happiness Reports) — Synthesize existing findings on the relative explanatory power of income, health, and social capital for subjective wellbeing, identifying whether the hypothesis is supported or contradicted by published evidence.

C008.subject: GDP per capita
C008.object: subjective wellbeing, health, and social cohesion
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita subjective wellbeing, health, and social cohesion]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and World Bank GDP per capita data (1990-2020) — Directly test the correlation by merging time-series data on GDP per capita with composite measures of subjective wellbeing, health, and social cohesion across OECD countries, controlling for confounders like inequality and institutional quality.

[PATH:literature] Easterlin Paradox literature review and meta-analysis (e.g., Easterlin et al., 2010; Stevenson & Wolfers, 2008) — Systematically assess existing evidence on the disputed relationship between income growth and wellbeing, focusing on OECD countries over the specified period, to identify whether the correlation holds or is moderated by threshold effects.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel studies (e.g., World Values Survey, European Social Survey) combined with health and social capital indices — Use individual-level panel data to examine within-country changes in GDP per capita and corresponding shifts in subjective wellbeing, health outcomes, and social cohesion, reducing ecological fallacy and testing causal direction.

C009.subject: Composite indices (e.g., HDI, GPI) that incorporate subjective wellbeing metrics (e.g., life satisfaction surveys)
C009.object: self-reported life evaluation across societies with high income inequality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Composite indices (e.g., HDI, GPI) that incorporate subjective wellbeing metrics (e.g., life satisfaction surveys) self-reported life evaluation across societies with high income inequality]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-national panel data analysis comparing predictive validity of HDI vs. GPI (including life satisfaction) for self-reported life evaluation in countries with high Gini coefficients (e.g., South Africa, Brazil, USA). — Directly tests whether adding subjective wellbeing metrics improves prediction of life evaluation in high-inequality contexts, using multilevel modeling to control for confounds.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental vignette study manipulating perceived income inequality and presenting either objective-only or subjective-inclusive composite indices to participants, then measuring subsequent self-reported life evaluation. — Isolates causal effect of composite index composition on life evaluation, addressing endogeneity concerns in observational data.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies comparing objective vs. subjective wellbeing indices' correlation with individual life satisfaction across inequality strata. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the hypothesis holds across different operationalizations and cultural contexts, identifying moderators like inequality level.

C010.subject: Composite indices (e.g., HDI, GPI)
C010.object: the complexity of human wellbeing across diverse societies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Composite indices (e.g., HDI, GPI) the complexity of human wellbeing across diverse societies]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative analysis of HDI vs. alternative multidimensional indices (e.g., OECD Better Life Index, Bhutan's GNH Index) across diverse developing countries, using survey data on subjective wellbeing and capabilities — Directly tests whether composite indices miss key dimensions (e.g., social relations, cultural values, environmental quality) by comparing their predictive power for self-reported wellbeing across different societal contexts.

[PATH:literature] Qualitative meta-analysis of ethnographic studies on wellbeing in non-Western societies, focusing on dimensions not captured by standard indices (e.g., spiritual fulfillment, community cohesion, autonomy) — Provides theoretical and empirical grounding for the hypothesis by identifying systematic omissions in composite indices, especially relevant for developing countries where cultural diversity is high.

qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on developing countries
